metals/aluminum.title: What does the evidence say about aluminum in people?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: An oral aluminum intake value
grade.basis: Two agencies published values, and the values are not the same weekly amount. The clinical-syndrome wording in the draft corpus was not verified, so it is not repeated here.

metals/aluminum.answerHtml: EFSA in 2008 set a tolerable weekly intake of 1 mg aluminum per kg body weight per week. ATSDR in 2008 set an intermediate and chronic oral minimal risk level of 1 mg aluminum per kg per day. Those two values are not the same weekly dose. The CDC National Report chemical list used for this site has no aluminum table.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
EFSA in 2008, recorded in the corpus from the abstract and the agency news page, set a tolerable weekly intake of 1 mg/kg body weight per week. EFSA 2008.

The corpus records an ATSDR 2008 intermediate and chronic oral minimal risk level of 1 mg Al/kg/day, taken from the minimal-risk-level table in the saved profile. It also records that a figure footnote in that PDF gives different numbers (0.3 and 0.9). This site uses the table value the corpus checked, and it does not treat the footnote as a second official value. ATSDR aluminum profile.

IARC, as cited by ATSDR 2008 and recorded in the corpus, classifies occupational aluminum production in Group 1. Whether aluminum metal itself is unclassified was not verified and is not stated. A WHO note that 0.1 mg/L or less is achievable at large treatment facilities is recorded via ATSDR. A 0.2 mg/L figure for small facilities was not verified and is not stated. WHO GDWQ.

A JECFA provisional tolerable weekly intake was marked unverified in the corpus because the WHO technical report was not opened. It is not stated here. No CDC National Report table for aluminum was in the chemical list checked for this corpus.

sections.heading: What is not in this corpus
sections.html: Vaccine aluminum quantities and a method for testing vaccine aluminum in people are not in the saved sources. Deferoxamine studies in dialysis patients are on the deferoxamine page. They are treatment series, not a population reference range.

metals/arsenic.title: What does the evidence say about arsenic in people?

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source
grade.outcome: Inorganic arsenic and cancer or cardiovascular endpoints
grade.basis: IARC Group 1, the EFSA 2024 reference point, the EPA 2025 reference dose, and the ATSDR chronic oral minimal risk level all address inorganic arsenic. Not graded A: these are assessments, not several randomized trials.

metals/arsenic.answerHtml: EPA's 2025 oral reference dose for inorganic arsenic is 0.00006 mg/kg/day, based on ischemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes, with an oral cancer slope factor of 32 per mg/kg/day for bladder and lung cancer. EFSA in 2024 used a skin-cancer reference point of 0.06 µg inorganic arsenic per kg body weight per day and did not set a tolerable daily intake. Total urine arsenic is a poor stand-in for inorganic exposure because arsenobetaine from seafood raises it.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
EPA IRIS, updated 13 January 2025, lists an oral reference dose of 6 x 10^-5 mg/kg/day for inorganic arsenic, based on ischemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes. The oral slope factor is 32 per mg/kg/day for bladder and lung cancer combined. The inhalation unit risk of 4.3 x 10^-3 per µg/m3 is the 1995 value, which the 2025 assessment did not update. EPA IRIS inorganic arsenic.

EFSA in 2024, recorded in the corpus as checked against the opinion, used a BMDL05 of 0.06 µg inorganic arsenic per kg body weight per day from skin cancer, also considered to cover lung cancer, and a margin-of-exposure approach with no tolerable daily intake. The corpus records that mean dietary exposures are in the range of that reference point. EFSA 2024.

The ATSDR 2007 profile, saved with this site, is cited in the corpus for a chronic oral minimal risk level of 0.0003 mg/kg/day (0.3 µg/kg/day) for inorganic arsenic. ATSDR arsenic profile. IARC classifies arsenic and inorganic arsenic compounds in Group 1. IARC volume 100C. A WHO drinking-water value was not verified and is not stated here.

Folic acid trials that change arsenic methylation are graded on the folic acid page. They are not evidence that folic acid removes stored arsenic.

metals/cadmium.title: What does the evidence say about cadmium in people?

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source
grade.outcome: Cadmium and kidney effects
grade.basis: EFSA and EPA both use a renal endpoint, and IARC classifies cadmium and its compounds in Group 1. The ATSDR oral value is from a draft profile. Not graded A.

metals/cadmium.answerHtml: EFSA set a cadmium tolerable weekly intake of 2.5 µg/kg body weight from a urinary cadmium reference point of 1 µg/g creatinine, with kidney tubular effects as the critical endpoint. EPA's oral reference doses, last updated in 1989, are 0.0005 mg/kg/day for water and 0.001 mg/kg/day for food, based on proteinuria. The ATSDR profile now posted is an October 2026 draft, so its minimal risk levels are provisional.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
EFSA in 2009, recorded in the corpus from the opinion abstract, set a tolerable weekly intake of 2.5 µg/kg body weight, derived from urinary cadmium of 1 µg/g creatinine. EFSA 2009.

EPA IRIS, last updated 1 October 1989, lists an oral reference dose of 5 x 10^-4 mg/kg/day for water and 1 x 10^-3 mg/kg/day for food, both for significant proteinuria. The inhalation unit risk is 1.8 x 10^-3 per µg/m3. The 1987 weight of evidence is B1, probable human carcinogen, based on limited human evidence. EPA IRIS cadmium.

The saved ATSDR cadmium file is labeled Draft for Public Comment, October 2026. The corpus records these draft minimal risk levels as checked against it: acute oral 0.002 mg/kg/day; no intermediate oral value; chronic oral 0.0003 mg/kg/day (0.3 µg/kg/day) from human renal data; acute inhalation 0.000002 mg/m3; chronic inhalation 0.0001 mg/m3. A 2012 final value of 0.1 µg/kg/day was not verified and is not used. The corpus also records a whole-body half-time of 20 to 30 years, with the kidney as the main storage organ. ATSDR cadmium draft.

IARC classifies cadmium and cadmium compounds in Group 1, as cited by the ATSDR draft and recorded in the corpus. IARC volume 100C. A WHO drinking-water value of 3 µg/L is recorded in the corpus as checked via that draft. WHO GDWQ. A JECFA monthly intake recorded only as a citation inside the draft is not restated here as a separate extraction.

metals/chromium.title: What does the evidence say about chromium in people?

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source
grade.outcome: Chromium(VI) carcinogenicity and oral reference dose
grade.basis: EPA IRIS (2024) and IARC Group 1 both classify chromium(VI) compounds as carcinogenic. The oral reference dose rests on a mouse study. Not graded A.

metals/chromium.answerHtml: EPA's August 2024 assessment sets a chromium(VI) oral reference dose of 0.0009 mg/kg/day based on small-intestine hyperplasia in female mice, and it describes chromium(VI) as carcinogenic to humans by inhalation and likely carcinogenic by the oral route. Chromium(III) is treated separately: EFSA set a tolerable daily intake of 0.3 mg/kg body weight per day in 2014. Most blood and urine chromium results in NHANES 2017 to 2018 were below the limit of detection.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
EPA IRIS, updated 1 August 2024, lists a chromium(VI) oral reference dose of 9 x 10^-4 mg/kg/day. The stated basis is hyperplasia in the small intestine of female mice. The lifetime oral slope factor is 0.27 per mg/kg/day, with an adult-based slope factor of 0.16 per mg/kg/day. The inhalation unit risk is 0.018 per µg/m3. EPA characterizes chromium(VI) as carcinogenic to humans by inhalation and likely to be carcinogenic to humans by the oral route. EPA IRIS chromium(VI).

The corpus records these ATSDR 2012 minimal risk levels as checked against the 2012 profile, which is not in the saved sources folder: chromium(VI) inhalation 0.000005 mg/m3 for intermediate and chronic aerosols or mists, and 0.0003 mg/m3 intermediate for particulates; chromium(VI) oral 0.005 mg/kg/day intermediate and 0.0009 mg/kg/day chronic; chromium(III) inhalation 0.005 and 0.0001 mg/m3 intermediate for insoluble and soluble particulates. ATSDR toxicological profiles.

EFSA in 2014, recorded from the abstract, set a chromium(III) tolerable daily intake of 0.3 mg/kg body weight per day. EFSA 2014. IARC, as cited by ATSDR 2012 and recorded in the corpus, places chromium(VI) compounds in Group 1 and metallic chromium and chromium(III) in Group 3. IARC volume 100C. A WHO drinking-water value for total chromium was not verified and is not stated here.

metals/cobalt.title: What does the evidence say about cobalt in people?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: A clinical blood-cobalt threshold
grade.basis: One European opinion gives a range rather than an exact threshold, and it states that systemic critical values are not established. Population percentiles are descriptive.

metals/cobalt.answerHtml: ATSDR's October 2024 profile sets an acute oral minimal risk level of 0.03 mg cobalt/kg/day and an intermediate oral level of 0.02 mg/kg/day. For metal-on-metal hips, SCENIHR said a whole-blood cobalt level for clinical concern was expected inside 2 to 7 µg/L and that the exact level was not determined. Critical values for systemic effects after those implants were not established.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
The saved ATSDR profile is dated October 2024. The acute oral minimal risk level of 0.03 mg Co/kg/day and the intermediate oral minimal risk level of 0.02 mg Co/kg/day were read from that file. The corpus also records inhalation minimal risk levels from the same profile: acute 0.0003 mg/m3, intermediate 0.00008 mg/m3, and chronic 0.0001 mg/m3. It records that WHO has no drinking-water guideline value for cobalt. ATSDR cobalt profile.

IARC 2023 groupings recorded in the corpus as checked against volume 131: cobalt metal without tungsten carbide, and soluble cobalt(II) salts, Group 2A; cobalt(II) oxide Group 2B; cobalt(II,III) oxide, cobalt(II) sulfide, and other cobalt(II) compounds Group 3. IARC volume 131. The corpus notes that cobalt is essential only as part of vitamin B12. Absorption wording beyond that was not re-extracted.

sections.heading: Metal-on-metal hips
sections.html:
SCENIHR in 2014 said screening should use whole blood, with cobalt as the reference substance. It said the threshold for clinical concern was expected within 2 to 7 µg/L cobalt in whole blood and that the exact level still had to be determined. Recommendations were based on local effects. Critical values for systemic effects had not been established. SCENIHR 2014.

The MHRA medical device alert MDA/2017/018, retrieved for this site, says there is no agreed whole-blood metal threshold that predicts outcome or mandates revision. It says rising blood metal levels may indicate potential for soft-tissue reaction, and that imaging should carry more weight than an isolated blood metal level. A figure of 7 ppb appears in the draft corpus but was not in the alert page retrieved here, so it is not stated as fact. MHRA MDA/2017/018.

metals/lead.title: What does the evidence say about lead in people?

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source
grade.outcome: Low-level lead and the lack of a current tolerable intake
grade.basis: CDC, EFSA, EPA, and ATSDR each address this from human data. There is no set of randomized trials, so the grade is not A.

metals/lead.answerHtml: CDC states that no safe blood lead level in children has been identified, and it set a blood lead reference value of 3.5 µg/dL that is a population marker, not a toxicity threshold. EFSA in 2010 did not set a new tolerable intake and published benchmark doses for developmental neurotoxicity, blood pressure, and kidney effects. EPA has not estimated an oral reference dose.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
CDC updated the blood lead reference value to 3.5 µg/dL. The saved MMWR page says 2.5 percent of U.S. children aged 1 to 5 years have a blood lead level at or above 3.5 µg/dL. CDC states that the value is not a health-based standard or a toxicity threshold, and that no safe blood lead level in children exists. The same page says venous blood is less likely to be contaminated than a skin prick. MMWR 2021.

EFSA in 2010, as recorded in the research corpus from the EFSA abstract, used a BMDL01 of 12 µg/L blood lead for developmental neurotoxicity, a BMDL01 of 36 µg/L for systolic blood pressure, and a BMDL10 of 15 µg/L for chronic kidney disease. The dietary equivalents recorded there are 0.50, 1.50, and 0.63 µg/kg body weight per day. EFSA judged the previous PTWI of 25 µg/kg body weight per week no longer appropriate and set no new health-based guidance value. EFSA 2010.

The ATSDR toxicological profile for lead (August 2020) derived no minimal risk levels. The corpus records, as checked against that profile, a blood elimination half-time of about 1 week to 2 years depending on age and exposure, and a bone half-time of about 1 to 2 decades, with bone holding most of the body burden. ATSDR lead profile.

EPA IRIS lists the oral reference dose for inorganic lead as information reviewed but value not estimated, last updated 8 July 2004. EPA IRIS lead. IARC, as cited by the ATSDR profile and recorded in the corpus, classifies inorganic lead compounds in Group 2A. The corpus records the evidence for organic lead compounds as inadequate, not as a Group 3 classification. IARC volume 87.

A provisional WHO drinking-water value of 10 µg/L is recorded in the corpus as checked via the ATSDR 2020 profile. WHO GDWQ. An FDA interim reference level was not opened in the corpus and is not stated here.

metals/mercury.title: What does the evidence say about mercury in people?

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source
grade.outcome: Methylmercury and neurodevelopment
grade.basis: EPA and the ATSDR methylmercury minimal risk level both use a neurodevelopmental basis, and EFSA published a methylmercury tolerable weekly intake. Not graded A, because this corpus does not contain several randomized trials.

metals/mercury.answerHtml: EPA set a methylmercury oral reference dose of 0.0001 mg/kg/day based on developmental neuropsychological impairment. EFSA set tolerable weekly intakes of 1.3 µg/kg body weight for methylmercury and 4 µg/kg body weight for inorganic mercury. Blood total mercury and blood methylmercury in NHANES 2017 to 2018 are reported below from the saved CDC tables. A hair-to-outcome relationship is established for methylmercury, not for most other substances.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:
EPA IRIS lists a methylmercury oral reference dose of 1 x 10^-4 mg/kg/day, last updated 27 July 2001, for developmental neuropsychological impairment. The page shows that value at both the high end and the low end of the BMDL05 range it cites. EPA IRIS methylmercury.

EFSA in 2012, recorded in the corpus from the abstract and the 20 December 2012 press release, set a tolerable weekly intake of 1.3 µg/kg body weight for methylmercury and 4 µg/kg body weight for inorganic mercury. EFSA 2012.

The corpus records these ATSDR 2024 minimal risk levels as checked against the mercury profile: chronic inhalation 0.3 µg Hg/m3 for elemental mercury; acute oral 2 µg Hg/kg/day for inorganic mercury; intermediate oral 0.01 µg Hg/kg/day for inorganic salts; chronic oral 0.1 µg Hg/kg/day for methylmercury. The profile PDF is not in the saved sources folder. The corpus states the bases as neurodevelopment for methylmercury, kidney effects for inorganic mercury, and neurological effects for elemental vapor. ATSDR toxicological profiles. Absorption fractions in that profile were not re-extracted and are not stated here.

IARC, as cited by ATSDR 2024 and recorded in the corpus, places methylmercury compounds in Group 2B and metallic and inorganic mercury in Group 3. IARC volume 58. A WHO drinking-water value for inorganic mercury was not verified and is not stated here.

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source

metals/nickel.answerHtml: EFSA in 2020 set a chronic tolerable daily intake of 13 µg nickel per kg body weight per day. Allergic contact dermatitis is the effect EFSA used for oral flare in sensitised people, as recorded from that opinion. sections.heading: Reference values
sections.html:

A WHO drinking-water value of 70 µg/L is recorded as cited in that EFSA opinion. EFSA 2020.

EPA IRIS, last updated 1 December 1991, lists an oral reference dose of 2 x 10^-2 mg/kg/day for soluble nickel salts, based on decreased body and organ weights. The cancer assessment says the information was reviewed but a value was not estimated. EPA IRIS nickel.

The corpus records ATSDR 2024 inhalation minimal risk levels of 0.0001 mg Ni/m3 (acute) and 0.000003 mg Ni/m3 (intermediate), checked against the 2024 profile, which is not in the saved sources folder. metals/titanium.title: What does the evidence say about titanium in people?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: Systemic titanium from implants or from E171
grade.basis: The food-additive conclusion is one EFSA opinion. The implant evidence is three small human series without a clinical outcome.

metals/titanium.answerHtml: EFSA in 2021 said a concern for genotoxicity of titanium dioxide (E171) could not be ruled out, and that E171 could no longer be considered safe as a food additive. Three small human studies found higher serum titanium in people with hip or spinal implants than in comparison groups. None of those studies measured a systemic health outcome from the titanium.

sections.heading: Food additive E171
sections.html: The corpus records two statements as checked against the EFSA 2021 opinion: a concern for genotoxicity could not be ruled out, and E171 can no longer be considered safe as a food additive. A statement that no acceptable daily intake was set was marked unverified and is not repeated. EFSA 2021. An IARC classification for titanium dioxide was not opened and is not stated.

sections.heading: Implants
sections.html:
Omlor and colleagues (2013) measured 67 patients and compared them with 11 people with non-modular implants and 23 people without implants. Both implant groups had higher serum titanium. The abstract called the absolute levels comparatively low. No systemic health outcome was measured. doi:10.1016/j.actbio.2012.12.001.

Cundy and colleagues (2014) followed 33 children with titanium-alloy spinal fusion. More than 95 percent of postoperative serum titanium and niobium levels were elevated, and levels correlated with implant surface area. Clinical implications were described as uncertain. doi:10.1007/s00586-014-3279-x.

Kasai and colleagues (2003) compared 46 spinal-implant patients with 20 controls. About one third had abnormal serum or hair metal values. Serum levels did not indicate implant failure. doi:10.1097/01.BRS.0000065482.41115.B4.

There is no validated clinical reference range for titanium in this corpus, and the CDC National Report list used here has no titanium table.

methodology.title: What does an evidence grade from A to F mean?

grade.title: No qualifying human study in this corpus
grade.outcome: This rubric as a research result
grade.basis: The rubric is a method. It is not itself a trial.

methodology.answerHtml: An A means several consistent human randomized trials for that outcome. An F means human evidence of no benefit for that outcome, or human evidence of harm. Grades between those follow study design, whether more than one human source agrees, and whether the result was replicated. If no qualifying human study was found, the grade is Not graded, which is not a finding of no effect.

sections.heading: Rubric
sections.html:
Grades attach to an outcome, not to a substance in the abstract. Succimer has a B for lowering blood lead and an F for cognitive benefit in the same trial. A chelator can change a lab number without changing health.

Folic acid is the only A. Two randomized trials agreed on arsenic methylation. A third paper is the same trial as the second and is not counted as a new replication.

Grades used on every outcome on this site
GradeMeaning
A Several consistent human randomized controlled trials for that outcome.
B At least one good human randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one independent agency or controlled study. Agency opinions are not graded A.
C A small or uncontrolled human study, a single limited trial, or one agency document.
D Case reports only, or conflicting human evidence.
F Human evidence of no benefit for the stated outcome, or human evidence of harm.
Not graded No qualifying human study in this corpus. This is not evidence of no effect.

sections.heading: Numbers
sections.html:
Every number on a page is tied to a named source with a DOI or an official URL. Where a draft table in the research corpus disagreed with a saved CDC PDF, the PDF figure is the one published. That happened for several urine percentiles. Blood lead, blood cadmium, blood mercury, blood methylmercury, blood cobalt, and blood chromium in the draft matched the saved tables and are published.

Claims marked unverified in the corpus, including some WHO drinking-water values, some half-time wording, and brand-level food tests, are not published. They are listed in the repository file research/unsourced-claims.md, which is not a page of this site.

questions/amalgam-removal.title: Is it safe to remove mercury amalgam fillings (and during pregnancy)?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: Routine removal of intact amalgam
grade.basis: FDA states a recommendation from its review. This corpus has no randomized trial of removal.

questions/amalgam-removal.answerHtml: FDA says it is not recommending that anyone remove or replace existing amalgam fillings in good condition unless removal is medically necessary, because removal can cause a temporary increase in mercury vapor and can remove healthy tooth. The same statement lists pregnancy among groups for whom new amalgam should be avoided when possible. From 1 January 2025, EU law says amalgam shall not be used for dental treatment in the Union except when a dentist judges it strictly necessary.

sections.heading: What the documents say
sections.html:
Higher-risk groups in the FDA statement include pregnant women and their fetuses, women planning pregnancy, nursing women and their infants, children especially under six, people with pre-existing neurological disease such as multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, or Parkinson disease, people with impaired kidney function, and people with known heightened sensitivity to mercury or other amalgam components. FDA, 24 September 2020.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1849 says that from 1 January 2025 dental amalgam shall not be used for dental treatment in the Union, except when deemed strictly necessary by the dental practitioner based on the specific medical needs of the patient. A derogation allows use until 30 June 2026 where amalgam is the only publicly reimbursed material at a rate of at least 90 percent. EUR-Lex.

A SCENIHR or SCHEER opinion on dental amalgam was not captured. It is not summarized.

questions/child-blood-lead.answerHtml: CDC's blood lead reference value is 3.5 µg/dL for children aged 1 to 5 years, equal to the level at or above which 2.5 percent of those children fall. sections.heading: What CDC states about the number

It points clinicians to CDC's recommended actions based on blood lead level. This site does not reprint a treatment plan. doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm7043a4.

In NHANES 2017 to 2018, children aged 1 to 5 years had a blood lead geometric mean of 0.670 µg/dL and a 95th percentile of 2.02 µg/dL (n=629), read from the saved CDC table. That row is population description, not a diagnosis.

questions/symptoms.title: What are the symptoms of heavy metal toxicity (adults, kids, toddlers)?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: One symptom pattern for heavy metal toxicity
grade.basis: The sourced material is a set of metal-specific endpoints from agency documents, not a diagnostic checklist study.

questions/symptoms.answerHtml: There is no single symptom list in this corpus that identifies heavy metal toxicity in adults or children. CDC states that no safe blood lead level in children exists. Other sourced endpoints are metal-specific: developmental effects for methylmercury, kidney effects for cadmium, skin and cancer endpoints for inorganic arsenic, and allergic contact dermatitis for nickel. Effects that were not re-checked against a saved source are not listed.

sections.heading: Endpoints that were verified
sections.html:
• Lead, children: CDC states that no safe blood lead level exists and that even low levels cause harm. The reference value is not a toxicity threshold. MMWR 2021.
  • Lead, EFSA 2010: developmental neurotoxicity, raised systolic blood pressure, and chronic kidney disease were the critical effects used for benchmark doses. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1570.
  • Methylmercury: EPA's reference dose is based on developmental neuropsychological impairment. The corpus records the ATSDR chronic oral minimal risk level basis as neurodevelopmental effects.
  • Inorganic mercury: the corpus records renal effects as the ATSDR minimal-risk-level basis. Elemental vapor: neurological effects, including tremor and erethism, as the inhalation basis.
  • Inorganic arsenic: EFSA 2024 used skin cancer as the critical endpoint. EPA's 2025 reference dose uses ischemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes. IARC Group 1 covers arsenic and inorganic arsenic compounds.
  • Cadmium: EFSA used kidney tubular dysfunction. EPA's reference dose uses proteinuria.
  • Nickel: the corpus records allergic contact dermatitis as the most common effect, and oral flare in sensitised people as the EFSA acute endpoint.
  • Chromium(VI): EPA describes it as carcinogenic to humans by inhalation and likely carcinogenic by the oral route. A longer symptom list from the 2012 profile was marked unverified and is not copied.

sections.heading: What is not listed
sections.html: Brain fog, a toddler behavior checklist, and a general detox symptom set were not outcomes in these documents. Cobalt systemic case descriptions and aluminum dialysis syndromes were marked unverified in the corpus and are not restated.

tests/blood-vs-urine-vs-hair.title: How do I test for heavy metals in my body (blood vs urine vs hair)?

grade.title: At least one good randomized trial, or consistent human evidence from more than one source
grade.outcome: One specimen for every metal
grade.basis: CDC, EFSA, ACMT, and the ATSDR hair panel agree that the specimen depends on the metal. They are agency positions, not randomized trials, so the grade is not A.

tests/blood-vs-urine-vs-hair.answerHtml: There is no single test for every metal. Venous whole blood lead is the CDC standard for lead. Urine cadmium, creatinine adjusted, is the marker EFSA used for kidney burden, and urine arsenic has to be speciated or seafood arsenobetaine will dominate the total. Hair can reflect methylmercury exposure. For most other substances, the ATSDR hair panel said a hair level does not predict a health effect.

sections.heading: What each specimen can and cannot tell you
sections.html:
• Blood lead: CDC uses venous whole blood. The 3.5 µg/dL reference value is a population marker for children aged 1 to 5 years, not a toxicity threshold. MMWR 2021.
  • Blood total mercury and blood methylmercury are measured in NHANES. The corpus did not verify a sentence that blood total mercury mainly reflects fish methylmercury, so that interpretation is not stated as fact here. The numbers are on the mercury page.
  • Urine cadmium: EFSA's reference point is 1 µg/g creatinine. EFSA 2009. Unadjusted µg/L percentiles are not that unit.
  • Urine arsenic: the saved CDC tables show a 2017 to 2018 total-arsenic 95th percentile of 61.5 µg/L and an inorganic-related-sum 95th percentile of 13.4 µg/L. Arsenobetaine's 95th percentile was 39.5 µg/L. Total arsenic without speciation mixes in seafood arsenobetaine.
  • Hair: the ATSDR panel said prediction of a health effect from hair is not supported for most substances. A relationship was agreed for methylmercury and, to a limited extent, arsenic, if external contamination is ruled out. Panel summary.
  • ACMT and AACT say not to use hair or nail testing to screen for metal poisoning in people with nonspecific symptoms. Choosing Wisely list.
  • A primary source for when to use a spot urine versus a 24-hour collection was not captured. This corpus does not state a rule for that choice.

tests/hair-mineral-analysis.title: Is hair mineral analysis (HTMA) accurate for heavy metals?

grade.title: Case reports only, or conflicting human evidence
grade.outcome: Hair mineral analysis as a general metal screen
grade.basis: Evidence conflicts by use. A research relationship exists for methylmercury. Screening people with nonspecific symptoms is discouraged by ACMT, and the panel found insufficient data for most substances.

tests/hair-mineral-analysis.answerHtml: For most substances, the ATSDR hair panel said there are not enough data to predict a health effect from the amount in hair. The panel agreed that a hair-to-outcome relationship was established for methylmercury and, to a limited extent, for arsenic, if external contamination is ruled out. ACMT and AACT say not to use hair or nail testing to screen for metal poisoning in people with nonspecific symptoms, because those tests are rarely required, frequently unreliable, and of limited use.

sections.heading: What the panel said
sections.html:
The summary statement was: for most substances, insufficient data exist to predict a health effect from the concentration in hair. Presence may indicate exposure, internal or external, and does not necessarily indicate the source. The panel said hair grows about 12 centimeters per year and is not generally useful for very recent exposures or for exposures longer ago than 1 year. The report says these are panelists' views, not ATSDR positions. Executive summary.

No clinical reference ranges for nails were captured. ACMT groups nails with hair for this screening use. Choosing Wisely PDF.

tests/mom-hip-ions.title: What can a cobalt or chromium blood test tell you after a metal-on-metal hip?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: A single cobalt or chromium number as a revision threshold
grade.basis: Agencies recommend considering the test in context. All three say an exact standalone threshold is not established.

tests/mom-hip-ions.answerHtml: SCENIHR said whole-blood cobalt in the range of 2 to 7 µg/L may mark a need for more investigation, and that the exact level inside that range was not determined. FDA says there is not enough evidence that one metal-ion number, by itself, shows a local lesion, a clinical outcome, or a need for revision. MHRA says there is no agreed whole-blood threshold that predicts outcome or mandates revision.

sections.heading: What the test can tell you
sections.html:
SCENIHR (2014) recommended whole blood, with cobalt as the reference substance. Additional imaging was recommended when cobalt was above a threshold inside 2 to 7 µg/L. Critical values for systemic effects were not established. SCENIHR PDF.

FDA says surgeons should consider metal-ion measurement in symptomatic patients, ideally in series, together with imaging and the clinical picture. FDA says evidence is insufficient to recommend testing when the patient has no signs or symptoms and the surgeon finds a well-functioning implant with normal radiographs. FDA recommends EDTA whole blood and a validated ICP-MS method able to measure as low as 1 µg/L for cobalt, and the same floor if chromium is measured. FDA says a metal-ion level in isolation has not been shown to correlate with localized lesions, clinical outcomes, or the need for revision. FDA testing page.

MHRA MDA/2017/018 says rising levels may indicate potential for soft-tissue reaction and that MARS MRI or ultrasound should carry more weight than an isolated blood level. MHRA alert.

sections.heading: What it cannot tell you
sections.html: It cannot, on these sources, serve as the only reason to revise an implant. Ordinary NHANES blood cobalt in 2017 to 2018 had a 95th percentile of 0.430 µg/L, which is below the SCENIHR concern range. That comparison is descriptive. It is not a diagnostic cutoff.

mainEntity.name: What can a cobalt or chromium blood test tell you after a metal-on-metal hip?

acceptedAnswer.text: SCENIHR said whole-blood cobalt in the range of 2 to 7 µg/L may mark a need for more investigation, and that the exact level inside that range was not determined. FDA says there is not enough evidence that one metal-ion number, by itself, shows a local lesion, a clinical outcome, or a need for revision. MHRA says there is no agreed whole-blood threshold that predicts outcome or mandates revision.

tests/provoked-urine.title: Is provoked (DMSA/DMPS challenge) urine testing valid?

grade.title: Human evidence of no benefit, or of harm
grade.outcome: Provoked urine as a test for metal poisoning
grade.basis: ACMT states that the test is not reliable and has been associated with harm. That is evidence against the claimed use, not a finding that chelators never change urine metals.

tests/provoked-urine.answerHtml: ACMT says not to give a chelating agent before a urine metal test. The Choosing Wisely text says chelators increase urinary metals even in healthy people without metal-related disease, and that provoked or challenge urine tests are not a reliable way to diagnose metal poisoning and have been associated with harm. A 2010 ACMT position statement, cited in the corpus, reaches the same conclusion: the practice is not validated, has no demonstrated benefit, and may be harmful.

sections.heading: What the statements say
sections.html:
The saved Choosing Wisely PDF says metals are ubiquitous and that storing some quantity of a metal is not the same as illness. It says administration of a chelator increases urinary excretion even without metal-related disease. Choosing Wisely PDF.

The corpus cites the ACMT position in Journal of Medical Toxicology 2010. doi:10.1007/s13181-010-0039-0. A sentence that unprovoked reference ranges do not apply to provoked samples was marked unverified in the corpus and is not repeated. Reference ranges from ordinary urine should not be assumed to fit a sample taken after a drug. This page does not state a numeric cutoff, because none was verified for provoked samples.

tests/urine.title: What can a urine metal test tell you?

grade.title: Small, uncontrolled, or single-source human evidence
grade.outcome: Urine as a general heavy-metal test
grade.basis: The cadmium reference point is one EFSA opinion. Speciation is shown by the NHANES distributions. Spot versus 24-hour guidance was not captured.

tests/urine.answerHtml: EFSA used creatinine-adjusted urine cadmium, with a reference point of 1 µg/g creatinine, as the basis for its cadmium tolerable weekly intake. Urine arsenic needs speciation: in NHANES 2017 to 2018 the total-arsenic 95th percentile was 61.5 µg/L and the inorganic-related sum was 13.4 µg/L. A primary source telling laboratories when to prefer a 24-hour collection over a spot sample was not in this corpus.

sections.heading: What urine can show
sections.html:
EFSA derived a tolerable weekly intake of 2.5 µg/kg body weight from urinary cadmium of 1 µg/g creatinine. EFSA 2009. The NHANES urine cadmium row on the cadmium page is in µg/L, not per gram of creatinine, so it is not that reference point.

The inorganic-related arsenic sum and arsenobetaine are separate CDC analytes. Using total urine arsenic alone counts seafood arsenobetaine. The 2017 to 2018 figures are on the arsenic page. They were read from the saved tables, not from an earlier draft table that did not match those files.

Urine cobalt, chromium, and nickel percentiles are on those metal pages. The corpus did not capture clinical reference ranges for 24-hour urine. Provoked urine, collected after a chelator, is a different test and is graded separately.
